title: Violin Sonata No. 9 in A major, “Kreutzer”
hook: A violin sonata written like a concerto, for a duel between two equal players.

painting.title: Ludwig van Beethoven with a Lyre-Guitar
painting.pairingNote: Beethoven as he looked in 1804–05, a year after he first played the sonata with George Bridgetower.

facts: Beethoven wrote the sonata in spring 1803 for George Bridgetower, a young virtuoso who had grown up in England and was visiting Vienna. They gave the first performance on 24 May 1803 in the Augarten, with Beethoven at the piano. The ink was barely dry: Bridgetower read the slow movement from Beethoven’s own copy, over his shoulder.

Beethoven’s working manuscript carries a joking dedication to Bridgetower. They later fell out; Bridgetower remembered a “silly quarrel about a girl”. When the sonata was published in Bonn in 1805, it was dedicated instead to Rodolphe Kreutzer, the leading French violinist. Kreutzer, according to Berlioz, never played it and found it unintelligible. His name stuck anyway.

Beethoven described it as written “in a very concertante style, almost like a concerto”. The violin and the piano are equals, and both parts are hard. The finale was first written for an earlier A major sonata, Op. 30 No. 1, and moved here.

In 1889 Leo Tolstoy named a novella after it, *The Kreutzer Sonata*, a dark story of jealousy in which the music sets off the drama. Janáček’s First String Quartet (1923) takes its title from Tolstoy’s story.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a slow door into a furious duel (I), a calm song and five variations (II), a whirling dance (III).

movements.heading: Adagio sostenuto – Presto
movements.summary: The violin begins alone, slowly, with full chords; the piano answers and the music darkens. Then a fierce Presto breaks out in A minor, a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] in which the two players trade blows. Only a quiet, hymn-like second theme brings relief.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: slow, rich chords on the violin alone, two or three notes at a time.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, Presto
mainIdeas.description: a short, rising figure that snaps into hard, clipped chords, passed between violin and piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a soft, hymn-like tune in long notes, in E major.

mainIdeas.name: The closing theme
mainIdeas.description: a driving, stamping tune in E minor that powers the end of each section.

stops.hear: The violin alone, slow and grand, playing full chords
stops.happening: The slow introduction. The violin opens with [[double-stop|double stop]]s

stops.hear: The piano answers with the same phrase; the harmony slides towards the minor and the music seems to stand still
stops.happening: Violin and piano in dialogue. Only the first bars are in A major

stops.hear: Sudden speed: a quick rising figure, then hard, short chords from both players
stops.happening: The Presto begins, in A minor

stops.hear: The storm stops for a quiet, slow-moving tune in long notes, like a hymn
A hammering, stamping tune drives forward
stops.happening: The closing theme, in E minor

stops.hear: The quick rising figure and hard chords from ≈ 1:10 again
The stamping tune is broken up and pushed through new keys
The music turns hushed and hesitant, stopping and starting on quiet chords
stops.happening: The tension gathers before the return

stops.hear: The opening Presto figure, back in A minor
Everything slows: a few bars of the slow music from the start

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Fast again, and a hard, final rush

notice: Listen to who leads. In the Presto the tune keeps jumping from violin to piano and back, often mid-phrase: neither player accompanies the other for long.
Notice how the quiet second theme moves in long, even notes while everything around it races. It sounds slower, though the tempo has not changed.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Perlman and Ashkenazy recorded the sonata in Kingsway Hall, London, in October 1973, as part of their complete Beethoven sonatas for Decca. They take the repeat of the exposition (≈ 3:35), which is why the movement lasts almost twelve minutes. On the Spotify album the sonata is tracks 1–3, followed by Sonata No. 10.

movements.heading: Andante con variazioni
movements.summary: After the storm, a gentle, singing tune in F major, followed by five [[variation|variation]]s. Each variation keeps the tune’s shape but dresses it differently: first the piano shines, then the violin, then the music turns dark and slow, before the light returns.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a calm, simple tune in two halves, each heard twice, shared between piano and violin.

mainIdeas.name: Variation 1
mainIdeas.description: the piano decorates the tune with [[trill|trill]]s over quick triplets; the violin adds little repeated notes.

mainIdeas.name: Variation 2
mainIdeas.description: the violin’s turn, with fast, glittering runs.

mainIdeas.name: Variation 3
mainIdeas.description: in F minor, slow and serious.

mainIdeas.name: Variation 4 and 5
mainIdeas.description: light filigree, then a broader, more searching ending.

stops.hear: A slow, gentle tune in the piano, then shared with the violin
The piano takes the lead with sparkling trills over quick notes in threes; the violin answers with short, repeated notes
The violin races in tiny, rapid notes while the piano keeps the tune’s outline
The light goes out: slower, darker, in the minor
Back to the major, with delicate, ornamented figures and trills in both instruments
The music slows almost to a halt, then the tune comes back, broad and changed
stops.happening: Into Variation 5, the longest, and a pause for breath

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Quiet, unhurried closing phrases

notice: Listen for the tune itself under the decoration. In every variation its outline and length stay the same, so you can always tell where you are in it.
Variation 3 is the only one in the minor. Notice how much darker the same tune sounds.

movements.heading: Finale. Presto
movements.summary: One loud piano chord, then a whirling dance in 6/8, like a [[tarantella|tarantella]]. The two players chase each other almost without pause; a few quieter, slower bars in two-time break the rhythm before the race starts again.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a quick, galloping tune in groups of three, tossed between violin and piano.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a smoother tune, interrupted by short passages in a slower two-time.

stops.hear: A single, loud chord on the piano, held
stops.happening: The signal to start, in A major

stops.hear: A galloping tune in quick threes, imitated from one instrument to the other
stops.happening: The main theme of the finale

stops.hear: A smoother tune; the rhythm suddenly changes for a few bars, slower and in two
stops.happening: The second theme, with the 2/4 interruptions

stops.hear: The galloping opening tune again
The tune is broken into pieces and tossed into new keys
The galloping tune at home in A major

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: A brief slowing, then a final dash and loud closing chords

notice: Listen for the moments where the 6/8 gallop stops and the music shifts into a slower two-time. They come like a held breath in the middle of the dance.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Perlman and Ashkenazy repeat the finale’s exposition. Recordings that leave it out, like Oistrakh and Oborin’s (about 7 minutes), are almost two minutes shorter.

threads.title: Two equals
threads.body: Beethoven’s own description, “almost like a concerto”, fits: there is no accompanist. The piano is as much a soloist as the violin, and the tunes keep changing hands.

threads.title: A minor and A major
threads.body: The sonata is called “in A major”, but the first movement’s main body is in A minor. Only the first bars and the finale belong to the major.

threads.title: Calm in the middle
threads.body: Between two fast, fierce movements stands a slow set of variations. The contrast is the shape of the whole piece.
